1.pericope_label: Set the trumpet to thy mouth. He shall come as an eagle against the house of the Lord
debates: Whether the house of the Lord is the temple or the people
What the trumpet command asks of the prophet
How the last word of the second verse is to be construed
outliers: Calvin sets himself against nearly all interpreters in denying that the house of God here means the temple
Ellicott hears irony in the title, since the calf itself was meant to symbolise Israel God
themes: A sentence with no verb in it
A prophet dressed as a herald of war
A name kept after the life has gone out of it
Knowledge of God that is only acquaintance

3.pericope_label: Israel hath cast off the thing that is good: the enemy shall pursue him
debates: What the thing that is good means
Whether the charge falls on the founding of the northern kingdom or on its later usurpers
What the clause I knew it not denies
outliers: Gill reports a rendering that reverses subject and object, so that the good One casts off Israel, and rejects it on the accents
Calvin makes kingdom and priesthood together the two images of Christ, so that overturning both is one apostasy
themes: A verb that means loathing something putrid
Good repelled and an enemy pursuing
A crown taken rather than given
Silver and gold spent on adorning a defection

5.pericope_label: Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off; mine anger is kindled against them
debates: Who casts off whom in the opening clause
Where the calf of Samaria stood
Whether the idolatry was invented or borrowed
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch denies there was ever a calf in the city itself and takes the name for the kingdom
Clarke reports a rendering that turns the clause into a command to put the calf away
themes: An idol carried off for the sake of its metal
A people the second time founders of one superstition
A workman who cannot make his own maker
A borrowed worship fitted to a home-made image

7.pericope_label: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk
debates: Whether sowing the wind means wasted labour or hypocritical pretence
What the useless vessel is
Why the swallowing is spoken of as already done
outliers: Calvin reads the sowing as an outward show indistinguishable from true worship but empty of faith
Keil and Delitzsch rests the whole advance of the threat on the tense of a single verb
themes: A harvest matched to its seed and multiplied
A crop denied at every stage in turn
A skin-bottle too foul to keep
Salt fit only to be walked on

9.pericope_label: For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers
debates: Whether going up to Assyria means embassy or captivity
Whether Israel is likened to the wild ass or contrasted with it
Who is gathered in the tenth verse and to what end
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch refuses to supply a word of likeness and makes the wild ass a contrast, since even that stupid animal keeps to itself
Ellicott takes the gathering as a restraint that leads to withheld tribute, and dates the non-payment a few years later
themes: A verb elsewhere used of going up to a sanctuary
An animal too swift for any hunter
Forces gathered from every side and heaped together
Payment made abnormally for one own shame

11.pericope_label: Because Ephraim hath made many altars to sin, altars shall be unto him to sin
debates: Whether the altars of the second clause are the same as those of the first
How men can build altars to sin without meaning to
What the great things of the law are
outliers: Clarke and Wesley take the second clause of altars they will be compelled to serve in captivity rather than those they built at home
Ellicott distinguishes the two uses of the same word, transgression in one clause and transgression with its guilt in the other
themes: Atonement attempted and offence committed at once
One altar required and many supplied
Error that hardens by simply lasting
A law inscribed and treated as no concern

13.pericope_label: They sacrifice flesh for the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat it; but the Lord accepteth them not
debates: What the disputed word in the opening clause means
Whether the return to Egypt is literal or figurative
How building temples can amount to forgetting God
outliers: Calvin reads the clause as a charge of turning burnt-offerings into meals so that nothing is wasted
Ellicott notes that the word used for these temples is elsewhere reserved for the Lord own house
themes: Gain quietly attached to superstition
A people back in Egypt without leaving home
Fenced cities counted in an enemy inscription
Remembrance that turns out to be forgetting
